title: Real-Time <i>in Vivo</i> Bacterial Imaging by Computed Tomography and Fluorescence Using Phage-Gold Nanorod Bioconjugates as Contrast Agents.

sections.heading: Step 1: Synthesis of Phanorod-ICG
sections.text:
Step 1: Synthesis of Phanorod-ICG 1-1. Resuspend the
phanorods (3.3 μM Au) in PBS buffer (pH 7.5). Add 5 mM ICG-NH 2  along with 5 mM NHS and 10 mM EDC into the buffer solution.
Add 10 mM EDC every 30 min twice and stir overnight. Critical Step EDC is rapidly hydrolyzed in water. Adding
EDC in this stepwise manner can improve the loading efficiency of
ICG onto the phanorods. 1-2. Purify the phanorod-ICG by dialysis
for 48 h in the dark. Collect the phanorod-ICG sample by centrifugation
(2000 rcf × 15 min). Critical Step Avoid excessive speed or duration of
centrifugation to prevent aggregation. If needed, the particles may
be concentrated by ultrafiltration.

Introduction Bacterial infections are an increasingly
significant concern in
medicine and public health. 
 , 
  The U.S. Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention estimates that antimicrobial resistant
infections were associated with more than 5 million deaths globally
in 2019  and are predicted to surpass cancer
as a leading cause of death by 2050. 
 , 
  Localized bacterial
accumulation, particularly in biofilms, is problematic due to increased
drug resistance and can lead to long-term contamination of implanted
materials. 
 − 
 
 
  Consequently, there is a growing need for methods to image bacterial
infections  in vivo . Conventional techniques for identifying
bacterial infection include culturing, polymerase chain reaction,
and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). 
 − 
 
 
 
 
  These methods are typically applied to patient samples and do not
give spatially resolved information. At the same time, nanomaterials
are increasingly used in biosensing. 
 − 
 
 
  Specifically, biosensors based
on quantum dots, 
 − 
 
  metal–organic frameworks, 
 − 
 
  and carbon
nanotubes 
 − 
 
  can be advantageous compared to conventional methods
in bacterial detection, exhibiting low detection limits, high sensitivity,
and low costs. To discriminate among bacterial species, nanoparticles
may be conjugated with targeting agents such as peptides, antibodies,
or phages. 
 − 
 
 
 
  Phages are viruses that infect bacteria and have therefore evolved
strong affinity and specificity to the host species during the ongoing
predator–prey evolutionary “arms race”. 
 − 
 
 
  Recently, phages have attracted wide attention for biomedical and
biotechnological applications due to their specificity, robustness,
and ease of production. 
 , 
  Compared with antibodies,
phages can be more robust in various chemical environments such as
serum, organic solvents, and even seawater. 
 − 
 
  Furthermore,
molecular engineering of phages includes both chemical modification
and genetic engineering, allowing alterations of host specificity
or range as well as loading of various cargo for detecting or treating
bacterial infections. 
 − 
 
 
 
 
 In previous work, phage-gold nanorod conjugates (“phanorods”)
were constructed through chemical conjugation of gold nanorods onto
the capsid of engineered phages derived from M13, a rod-shaped phage
that normally infects F+ strains of  Escherichia coli  ( E. coli ). 
 , , 
  By swapping the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of
the wild-type M13 g3p protein, the phages and phanorods could be selectively
retargeted toward other bacterial pathogens. The phanorods were used
for photothermal therapy of infected wounds in a preclinical mouse
model, taking advantage of the strong surface plasmon resonance (SPR)
absorption by gold nanorods and subsequent conversion to heat. Irradiation
with near-infrared (NIR) light killed the bacterial cells and led
to effective wound treatment.  In a similar
application, phages conjugated to gold nanoparticles could be used
for bacterial detection  in vitro , as attachment to
bacterial cells caused changes in the SPR absorbance spectrum, leading
to a visible color change.  Engineering
the RBD allowed retargeting to several different host species. At
the same time, the potential for using engineered M13 phages to detect
bacteria  in vivo  was previously demonstrated by fluorescence
imaging, in which phages were labeled by Alexa Fluor 750 dye;  NIR imaging, in which phages were labeled with
carbon nanotubes;  and recently magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI), in which phages were loaded with the contrast
agent Mn 2+ .  Thus, M13 phage
derivatives carrying a variety of detectable cargoes represent a promising
class of agents for  in vivo  imaging. A detailed
protocol for construction of phanorods has been presented
elsewhere.  Here, we describe step-by-step
protocols for validating the construction of phanorods as well as
their use as imaging probes for bacterial infections in mice. We describe
two imaging modalities: first, computed tomography (CT) imaging using
phanorods and, second, fluorescence imaging enabled by conjugation
of phanorods with indocyanine green (ICG) via carbodiimide cross-linking
chemistry. We further describe protocols for initial assessment of  in vitro  and  in vivo  toxicity of phanorod
probes.

Method 1: Validation of Phanorod Construction with Qubit Fluorometer Transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) is an excellent method to
confirm phanorod morphology, as previously demonstrated, 
 , 
  but requires training and instrument access.  It is therefore desirable to validate phanorod construction
via a simpler method before TEM. Briefly, phanorods are constructed
by incubating 200 μL of
thiolated phages (at 10 11  virions/mL) with 1 mL of gold
nanorods, allowing gold–sulfur bonds to form. Bioconjugates
are centrifuged, and the pellet is collected and resuspended in 200
μL of water, with unbound phages discarded with the supernatant.  The presence of gold nanorods in solution is
apparent due to their unique colorimetric properties, but their optical
absorbance interferes with spectroscopic methods normally used to
detect the phage. In particular, phage concentration can be quantified
by measuring the absorbance at 269 and 320 nm, using the equation  
 v i r i o n s m L = ( A 269 − A 320 ) × 6 × 10 16 n u m b e r of b a s e s p h a g e g e n o m e 
 , or by fluorescent staining of the viral
single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).  To avoid
this interference, the protocol described below first isolates the
ssDNA from the phanorods before quantitation. Using buffers
from commercially available MiniPrep kits, the phages
in the phanorod pellet are chemically denatured, and DNA is isolated.
Centrifugation separates the ssDNA, remaining in the supernatant,
from the gold nanorods that are included in the pellet. To minimize
the loss of ssDNA, the phage DNA is concentrated by speed vacuum centrifugation
rather than MiniPrep columns. Using a Qubit Fluorometer, amounts as
small as 10 pg/μL phage DNA are detected. This method should
be adaptable to other M13 derivatives, since it does not depend on
the genome sequence (e.g., unlike qPCR), and may be applicable to
other types of conjugates that can be separated by centrifugation.
This preliminary validation method does not absolve the experimenter
of the need for TEM or other detailed characterization but rather
is a potential time-saving step to introduce when there is uncertainty
regarding success of phanorod preparation (e.g., when troubleshooting
production from a new construct or optimizing conditions). Materials Reagents ZymoPURE P1 (Red) buffer (Zymo Research, D4200-1) ZymoPURE P2 (Blue) buffer (Zymo Research,
D4200-2) ZymoPURE P3 (Yellow) buffer
(Zymo Research, D4200-3) Qubit ssDNA
Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Q10212) Qubit Assay Tubes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Q32856) 1.5 mL Eppendorf DNA LoBind Tubes (Eppendorf, 022431021) Equipment Benchtop centrifuge Qubit
4 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Q33226) Vacuum Concentrator Overview Step 1: Extraction of Phanorod ssDNA Step 2: Concentrate ssDNA Step 3: Detection of ssDNA by Qubit Fluorometer Step 1: Extraction of Phanorod ssDNA (1 h) 1-1. Centrifuge
200 μL of phanorods (at a concentration ≤ 10 11  virions/mL) for 30 min at 5510 rcf in a 1.5 mL tube. Discard supernatant
and resuspend pelleted phanorods in 250 μL of ZymoPURE P1 (Red)
buffer. 1-2. Prepare a standard curve. Adjust phage concentration
to 10 13  virions/mL in 1× PBS and perform 2-fold serial
dilutions, down to a concentration of 3.13 × 10 11  virions/mL.
Add 25 μL of each dilution to 225 μL of ZymoPURE P1 (Red)
buffer. 1-3. Prepare a blank sample by adding 250 μL of
ZymoPURE
P1 (Red) buffer to a 1.5 mL tube. 1-4. To all samples, add 250
μL of ZymoPURE P2 (Blue) and
mix by inverting the tube ten times. Avoid vortexing throughout this
step. Incubate for 3 min at room temperature. Add 250 μL of
ZymoPURE P3 (Yellow) and invert to mix. Once the solution has turned
completely yellow, invert an additional five times. Centrifuge the
solution for 10 min at 16,000 rcf. Transfer 600 μL of DNA-containing
supernatant to a clean 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube. Critical Step In Step 1-1, avoid centrifuging the phanorods
at a high speed (e.g., >25,000 rcf) or for a long period (e.g.,
>1
h) to prevent formation of aggregates that may be difficult to resuspend.
In Steps 1–4, avoid disturbing the pellet while removing the
supernatant, as any gold nanorods will interfere with the later fluorescence
measurement. Step 2A: Concentrate ssDNA: Speed Vacuum (2 h) With
the drying rate set to high, use a vacuum concentrator to reduce the
sample volume to 25–50 μL. Drying time will vary; in
our experience, this step requires approximately 1.5 h. Check sample
volume after 1 h and every 15 min after. OR Step 2B: Concentrate ssDNA: Ethanol Precipitation (Overnight
Incubation + 40 min) If a speedvac is not available, then
ethanol precipitation can be used as an alternative. Split the supernatant
evenly between two 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes, and add 2.5 volumes
of 100% ethanol (750 μL) to each tube. Incubate overnight at
−20 °C. The following day, centrifuge at 16,000 rcf for
30 min. Discard the supernatant, air-dry on the benchtop, and resuspend
each pellet in 15–25 μL of water and combine. Critical Step The DNA pellets may be difficult or impossible
to see by visual inspection. Note the orientation of the tubes and
expected location of the pellet before the supernatant is removed
to avoid disturbing the pellet. While the yield may be lower in Step
2B compared to Step 2A, in Step 2B there is no interference from the
ZymoPURE buffers after resuspending the pellet in water, and a blank
sample (water) will show little signal in the following step. Step 3: Detection of ssDNA by Qubit Fluorometer (15 min) Using 20 μL of sample, follow the manufacturer’s instructions
to quantify the amount of ssDNA present using a Qubit Fluorometer.
If Step 2A was used, make sure to subtract the measurement of the
blank sample (e.g., “ng/μL”) from the phanorod
sample and standard curve to account for the signal from the ZymoPURE
buffers. Critical Step Optimal Qubit readings are achieved at
room temperature (22–28 °C). Avoid taking multiple consecutive
repeat readings of the same assay tube, as the local temperature may
rise, resulting in a temporary reduction in fluorescence. Similarly,
excessive manual handling of the tubes and exposure to body heat can
induce the same effect. 
 Troubleshooting Sample Precipitates during Speed Vacuum Concentration Add 20 μL of water and vortex or sonicate the sample until
solubilized, adding more water if necessary. Note that, while ZymoPURE
buffers are fairly resistant to precipitation, in our experience,
lysis and neutralization buffers from other commercially available
miniprep kits may be difficult to concentrate below 100 μL. ssDNA Is Too Low to Detect Concentrate the sample further
using the speed vacuum or use a larger volume of phanorods initially.
Additionally, if gold nanorods are not sufficiently removed during
centrifugation steps, they can interfere with fluorescence measurement
later. To determine if this is a potential problem, 1 mL of gold nanorods
may be centrifuged and resuspended in 250 μL of ZymoPURE P1
buffer, following the remaining protocol steps. If the resulting measurement
is substantially lower than that of the blank, gold nanorod contamination
was likely to be present in previous samples. ssDNA Is Too High to Detect Redo the Qubit assay using
less sample, i.e., 10 or 1 μL, or dilute samples if necessary.
Note that the presence of ZymoPURE buffers increases the fluorescence
signal, so samples may reach the quantitation limit at a lower concentration
than expected. Anticipated Results Three samples of phanorods were
prepared following the previously published protocol.  After centrifuging and resuspending the phanorods in 250
μL of P1 buffer during Step 1-1, the maximum concentration can
be no higher than 8 × 10 10  virions/mL with 100% conjugation
efficiency. Triplicate samples of phage at a known concentration (10 11  virions/mL) and gold nanorods were also prepared. Resulting
ssDNA concentrations, in ng/μL, were determined, and the value

Method 2:  In Vivo  Bacterial Imaging by CT Using
Phanorods CT imaging depends on differences in X-ray attenuation
among tissues
and bodily locations. Gold nanomaterials have been proposed as next-generation
contrast agents due to the high atomic number of gold, enabling lower
radiation doses, along with the chemical inertness of gold.  By delivering gold nanorods to the bacterial
cells, phanorods can create radiodensity at localized infection sites.
Here, phanorods are used to image the site of a localized injection
of 1 × 10 8  colony-forming units (CFUs) of bacterial
cells. The phanorods were administered by tail vein injection 24 h
post-infection. The specificity of the phanorods is demonstrated by
the contrast between a bolus of targeted ( P. aeruginosa ) and nontargeted ( V. cholerae ) cells imaged
simultaneously. Materials Reagents Phosphate buffered saline (PBS) (Sigma-Aldrich, P3813) 
 Pseudomonas aeruginosa  (ATCC25102
(Schroeter)
Migula) 
 Vibrio cholerae  0395 (donation from
Prof. Michael J. Mahan, UCSB) Equipment CrumpCAT CT scanner: 50 kVp, 200 μA, 200 μm
resolution (developed at the UCLA Crump Institute for Molecular Imaging) Overview Step 1: Anesthesia Step
2: Bacterial infection and phanorod injection Step 3: CT imaging Step 1: Anesthesia (30 min) 1-1. Weigh the mouse and
place it in an induction chamber with 2% isoflurane gas in oxygen.
Once general anesthesia is induced, the animal is removed from the
induction chamber and attached securely to a nose cone. 1-2.
Maintain body temperature at 37 °C with a heat pad. Step 2: Bacterial Infection and Phanorod Injection (24 h) 2-1. Prior to injection, the skin was sterilized with isopropyl
alcohol. 2-2. Inject 10 8  CFU  P. aeruginosa  in 0.5 mL of PBS buffer into the right caudal thigh muscle of the
animal to induce myositis. Inject 0.5 mL of 10 8  CFU  V. cholerae  into the left caudal thigh muscle of the
mouse as a control. 2-3. 24 h post-infection, inject the phanorods
(Au concentration
= 3.3 μM) intravenously (IV) into the tail vein. Critical Step Handle the phanorod solution gently and
do not sonicate or vortex vigorously. For IV injection, phanorods
should be handled under sterile conditions and resuspended in a sterile
buffer. Depending on the specific phanorods’ sensitivity to
storage, phanorods might be frozen and/or lyophilized or refrigerated
until use. Precipitates may be observed after long-term storage, which
may be possible to resuspend by gentle pipetting. Storage conditions
of a specific phanorod will depend on the stability of the engineered
phage and thus should be optimized for each type. Step 3: CT Imaging (48 h) CT imaging is performed at
time points after injection, depending on the infection model. 3-1. Place the mouse on the animal bed in the CrumpCAT microCT scanner.
To minimize movement artifacts, mice were placed in an imaging chamber
with provision for air and exhaust and with heating to maintain the

Using Phanorod-ICG While CT imaging has excellent tissue

volume (MCV), platelet count, white blood cell count (WBC), red cell
distribution width (RDW), and red blood cell count (RBC) were measured

± standard deviations ( n  = 3).

Conclusion We present methods for  in vivo  targeting and imaging
of bacterial infections with phage-based probes. M13 phage is first
engineered to bind the desired target (e.g.,  P. aeruginosa ) via replacement of the receptor-binding domain. Next, gold nanorods
are conjugated, producing phanorods, which give intrinsic CT contrast.
Cross-linking fluorescent dyes to the phanorod gives probes for fluorescence
imaging. While the gold nanorods and ICG dye serve as contrast agents
for CT and fluorescence imaging, respectively, the engineered phage
provides the specific targeting ability  in vivo ,
potentially distinguishing among bacterial species depending on the
design. Evaluation of  in vitro  and  in vivo  toxicity is also necessary for  in vivo  imaging
probes, and we describe protocols for initial assessment of toxicity.
These methods may be useful for spatial mapping of bacterial infections  in vivo  for both basic research and biomedical applications.
